course.title: Introduction and History · The Superposition Principle

unit.title: Qubits, superposition and inner products
unit.date: Notes: Introduction and History · The Superposition Principle
unit.intro: What a quantum state is, why amplitudes (not probabilities) are the basic objects, and how inner products give measurement probabilities.

steps.title: States are unit vectors
steps.md:
A **qubit** is a two-level quantum system. Its state is a unit vector in $\mathbb{C}^2$:
$$|\psi\rangle = \alpha|0\rangle + \beta|1\rangle, \qquad |\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1.$$
The complex numbers $\alpha, \beta$ are **amplitudes**. A $d$-level system (a *qudit*; $d=3$ is a qutrit) works the same way with $d$ basis states.

Two facts that trip people up:

- **Global phase is invisible.** $|\psi\rangle$ and $e^{i\gamma}|\psi\rangle$ give identical predictions for every experiment.
- **Relative phase is not.** $|+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)$ and $|-\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle - |1\rangle)$ differ only by the sign of one amplitude, yet they are perfectly distinguishable.

Other states worth memorizing: $|{\pm i}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle \pm i|1\rangle)$.

q.name: N1
q.prompt: For the state $c\,(|0\rangle + 2i\,|1\rangle)$ to be normalized, what must $|c|$ be?
q.why: The squared magnitudes of the amplitudes are $|c|^2(1 + |2i|^2) = 5|c|^2$, so $|c| = 1/\sqrt5$. Note $|2i|^2 = 4$, not $-4$.

q.name: N2
q.prompt: Which pair of states can **no** experiment tell apart?
q.why: $-|+\rangle = e^{i\pi}|+\rangle$ differs from $|+\rangle$ only by a global phase. Every other pair differs by a relative phase or is orthogonal.

steps.title: Photon polarization: superposition you can see
steps.md:
Polarization is a convenient physical qubit: write horizontal as $|0\rangle$ (or $|H\rangle$) and vertical as $|1\rangle$. Light polarized at angle $\theta$ is
$$|\theta\rangle = \cos\theta\,|0\rangle + \sin\theta\,|1\rangle.$$
An ideal polarizing filter at angle $\phi$ *measures* in the basis $\{|\phi\rangle, |\phi + 90^\circ\rangle\}$: a photon passes with probability $|\langle\phi|\theta\rangle|^2 = \cos^2(\theta - \phi)$, and if it passes it **is now** polarized at $\phi$.

That last clause is what makes the three-filter puzzle work: two crossed filters block everything, but inserting a third filter between them lets light through, because the middle filter re-prepares each photon in a new state.

q.name: N3
q.prompt: Horizontally polarized photons pass through filters at $22.5^\circ, 45^\circ, 67.5^\circ, 90^\circ$ in that order. What fraction comes out the end?
q.why: Each filter is $22.5^\circ = \pi/8$ past the last one, so each passes $\cos^2(\pi/8)$ of the photons reaching it. Four filters give $\cos^8(\pi/8)$. More, finer steps let *more* light through; in the limit the light is rotated with no loss.

steps.title: Inner products and bases
steps.md:
The inner product of $|\phi\rangle = \sum_i \phi_i|i\rangle$ and $|\psi\rangle = \sum_i \psi_i |i\rangle$ is
$$\langle\phi|\psi\rangle = \sum_i \phi_i^{*}\,\psi_i .$$
The **bra** $\langle\phi|$ is the conjugate transpose of the ket, so don't forget the complex conjugate.

An **orthonormal basis** $\{|v_0\rangle,\dots,|v_{d-1}\rangle\}$ satisfies $\langle v_i|v_j\rangle = \delta_{ij}$. Measuring $|\psi\rangle$ in that basis gives outcome $i$ with probability
$$p_i = |\langle v_i|\psi\rangle|^2,$$
and these sum to 1 because $\sum_i |v_i\rangle\langle v_i| = I$ (the **completeness relation**).

q.name: N4
q.prompt: Measure $|\psi\rangle = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|0\rangle + \tfrac12|1\rangle$ in the $\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis. What is the probability of the outcome $+$?
q.why: $\langle +|\psi\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} + \tfrac12\right)$, so $p_+ = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{(\sqrt3+1)^2}{4} = \tfrac{4 + 2\sqrt3}{8} = \tfrac{2+\sqrt3}{4}$.

q.name: N5
q.prompt: What is $|\langle +|{+i}\rangle|^2$?
q.why: $\langle +|{+i}\rangle = \tfrac12(1 + i)$, whose squared magnitude is $\tfrac14\cdot 2 = \tfrac12$. The $x$- and $y$-bases are *mutually unbiased*: either basis's states give 50/50 outcomes in the other.

q.name: N6
q.prompt: A qutrit in $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(|0\rangle+|1\rangle+|2\rangle)$ is measured in the basis $\{|0\rangle,\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|1\rangle+|2\rangle),\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|1\rangle-|2\rangle)\}$. Probability of the second outcome?
q.why: The overlap is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1+1) = \tfrac{2}{\sqrt6}$; squared, $\tfrac46 = \tfrac23$. The third outcome has probability 0 and the first $\tfrac13$.

course.title: Unitary Evolution and the Bloch Sphere

unit.title: Unitary evolution and the Bloch sphere
unit.date: Notes: Unitary Evolution and the Bloch Sphere
unit.intro: Closed systems evolve by unitary matrices; for one qubit, every unitary is a rotation of the Bloch sphere.

steps.title: Unitary evolution
steps.md:
An isolated system evolves linearly and preserves normalization, so the evolution is a **unitary** matrix: $U^\dagger U = I$. Unitaries preserve all inner products and are always reversible ($U^{-1} = U^\dagger$).

The workhorse one-qubit gates:
$$X = \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\ Y = \begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\ Z = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\ H = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
$X$ flips $|0\rangle \leftrightarrow |1\rangle$, $Z$ flips the sign of $|1\rangle$, and $H$ swaps the $Z$ basis with the $X$ basis: $H|0\rangle = |+\rangle$, $H|1\rangle = |-\rangle$. Also useful: the phase gate $S = \mathrm{diag}(1, i)$ and $T = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4})$.

steps.title: The Bloch sphere
steps.md:
Up to global phase, every qubit state can be written
$$|\psi\rangle = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,|0\rangle + e^{i\varphi}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle,$$
which we draw as the point $(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta)$ on the unit sphere.

- $|0\rangle$ is the north pole and $|1\rangle$ the south pole.
- $|\pm\rangle$ sit at $\pm x$ and $|{\pm i}\rangle$ at $\pm y$.
- **Orthogonal states are antipodal.** Note the half-angle: a $90^\circ$ angle in Hilbert space is $180^\circ$ on the sphere.
- Measuring in the standard basis gives $0$ with probability $\cos^2(\theta/2) = (1+z)/2$.

q.name: B1
q.prompt: What is the Bloch-sphere $z$-coordinate of $\cos\tfrac{\pi}{8}|0\rangle + \sin\tfrac{\pi}{8}|1\rangle$?
q.why: Here $\theta/2 = \pi/8$, so $\theta = \pi/4$ and $z = \cos\theta = 1/\sqrt2$. The point is halfway between $|0\rangle$ (north pole) and $|+\rangle$ (the equator).

steps.title: Gates are rotations
steps.md:
The rotation gates
$$R_z(\alpha) = \begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\alpha/2}&0\\0&e^{i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_x(\alpha) = e^{-i\alpha X/2},\qquad R_y(\alpha) = e^{-i\alpha Y/2}$$
rotate the sphere by angle $\alpha$ about the named axis. In general $R_{\hat n}(\alpha) = \cos\tfrac{\alpha}{2}I - i\sin\tfrac{\alpha}{2}(\hat n\cdot\vec\sigma)$.

Every one-qubit unitary is, up to global phase, a rotation of the Bloch sphere. The Paulis are $180^\circ$ rotations about $x$, $y$, $z$. $H$ is a $180^\circ$ rotation about the axis halfway between $x$ and $z$, so it swaps $x \leftrightarrow z$ and sends $y \to -y$. $S$ is a $90^\circ$ rotation about $z$.

> A **reflection** of the sphere (for example $z \to -z$ with $x, y$ fixed) is *not* a rotation, so no unitary does it.

q.name: B2
q.prompt: What does the phase gate S = diag(1, i) do to |+⟩?
q.why: $S|+\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle + i|1\rangle) = |{+i}\rangle$: a quarter turn about $z$ carries $+x$ to $+y$.

options: Swaps the x and z axes and reverses y
Swaps x and y and reverses z
q.soln: Swaps the x and z axes and reverses y
q.name: B3
q.prompt: What does H do to the Bloch sphere?
q.why: $H$ is a half-turn about $(\hat x + \hat z)/\sqrt2$. That swaps $\hat x$ and $\hat z$ and, like any half-turn, sends the perpendicular axis $\hat y$ to $-\hat y$.

q.name: B4
q.prompt: A qubit's Bloch vector makes a $120^\circ$ angle with the $+z$ axis. What is the probability that a standard-basis measurement gives $0$?
q.why: $P(0) = \cos^2(\theta/2) = \cos^2 60^\circ = \tfrac14$. Equivalently $z = \cos 120^\circ = -\tfrac12$ and $(1+z)/2 = \tfrac14$.

q.name: B5
q.prompt: On the Bloch sphere, what is the angle (in degrees) between $|0\rangle$ and $|-\rangle$?
q.why: $|0\rangle$ is the north pole and $|-\rangle$ is on the equator at $-x$, so they are $90^\circ$ apart on the sphere, though their Hilbert-space overlap is $1/\sqrt2$, a $45^\circ$ angle.

unit.title: Measurements and observables
unit.intro: Von Neumann (projective) measurements, observables and expectation values, and why non-orthogonal states can't be perfectly distinguished.

steps.title: Projective measurements
steps.md:
A **von Neumann measurement** is given by an orthonormal basis, or more generally by orthogonal projectors $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_m$ with $\sum_k \Pi_k = I$. On state $|\psi\rangle$:
$$P(k) = \langle\psi|\Pi_k|\psi\rangle, \qquad |\psi\rangle \mapsto \frac{\Pi_k|\psi\rangle}{\sqrt{P(k)}}.$$
When a projector has rank > 1, the measurement only learns which *subspace* the state is in. The state is projected onto it, keeping its shape within the subspace instead of collapsing all the way to a basis vector.

steps.title: Observables
steps.md:
An **observable** is a Hermitian matrix $M = \sum_k \lambda_k \Pi_k$ (its spectral decomposition). Measuring $M$ means doing the projective measurement $\{\Pi_k\}$ and reporting the eigenvalue $\lambda_k$. The average outcome is
$$\langle M\rangle = \sum_k \lambda_k P(k) = \langle\psi|M|\psi\rangle.$$
If an eigenvalue is repeated, its $\Pi_k$ projects onto the whole eigenspace. Example: $Z = |0\rangle\langle0| - |1\rangle\langle1|$, so $\langle Z\rangle = |\alpha|^2 - |\beta|^2$, which is the Bloch $z$-coordinate.

q.name: M1
q.prompt: For $|\psi\rangle = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}|0\rangle + \tfrac12|1\rangle$, what is $\langle Z\rangle$?
q.why: $\langle Z\rangle = \tfrac34 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac12$.

q.name: M2
q.prompt: For the same state, what is $\langle X\rangle$?
q.why: $\langle X\rangle = 2\,\mathrm{Re}(\alpha^*\beta) = 2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. As a check, $\langle X\rangle^2 + \langle Z\rangle^2 = 1$: the state is on the $xz$ great circle.

steps.title: Distinguishing states
steps.md:
Two states can be told apart *perfectly* only if they are orthogonal. For two equally likely pure states $|\psi_0\rangle, |\psi_1\rangle$, the best possible success probability (Helstrom's bound) is
$$P_{\text{succ}} = \tfrac12\left(1 + \sqrt{1 - |\langle\psi_0|\psi_1\rangle|^2}\right).$$
More general measurements (**POVMs**) can sometimes beat every projective measurement on the original system. Physically, a POVM is just a projective measurement on the system *plus an ancilla*: append a qubit in $|0\rangle$, apply a unitary, then measure. This is the trick for identifying one of three symmetric qubit states.

options: Yes: measure in the X basis
Yes: measure in the Z basis
Yes, but only with a POVM
q.name: M3
q.prompt: Can any measurement distinguish |0⟩ from |+⟩ with certainty?
q.why: $\langle 0|+\rangle = 1/\sqrt2 \ne 0$. Helstrom's bound gives at most $\tfrac12(1 + 1/\sqrt2) = \cos^2(\pi/8) \approx 0.854$, and ancillas don't change that.

q.name: M4
q.prompt: An observable has eigenvalue $2$ on $|0\rangle$ and $-1$ on $|1\rangle$. What is its expectation value in the state $|+\rangle$?
q.why: $\tfrac12(2) + \tfrac12(-1) = \tfrac12$.

q.name: M5
q.prompt: A qutrit in (|0⟩+|1⟩+|2⟩)/√3 is measured with projectors Π₁ = |0⟩⟨0| and Π₂ = |1⟩⟨1| + |2⟩⟨2|. If the outcome is Π₂, what is the new state?
q.why: Projecting gives $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(|1\rangle + |2\rangle)$, and renormalizing gives $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|1\rangle+|2\rangle)$. A rank-2 projector does **not** pick out $|1\rangle$ or $|2\rangle$; the superposition survives.

course.title: Joint Quantum Systems and Tensor Products · More Tensor Products

unit.title: Tensor products and entanglement
unit.date: Notes: Joint Quantum Systems and Tensor Products · More Tensor Products
unit.intro: Composite systems live in the tensor product. Learn to recognize entanglement and to compute what happens when you measure one part.

steps.title: Combining systems
steps.md:
The state space of two systems is the **tensor product**: dimensions multiply, so $n$ qubits need $2^n$ amplitudes. Basis states are written $|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle = |a\rangle|b\rangle = |ab\rangle$.

Operators act factor by factor: $(A\otimes B)(|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle) = A|a\rangle \otimes B|b\rangle$. As matrices, $A\otimes B$ is the **Kronecker product**: each entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ becomes the block $a_{ij}B$. Order matters, and the convention is that the first factor is the most significant bit.

steps.title: Entanglement
steps.md:
A two-qubit state is a **product state** if it equals $|u\rangle\otimes|v\rangle$, and **entangled** otherwise. For
$$|\psi\rangle = a|00\rangle + b|01\rangle + c|10\rangle + d|11\rangle,$$
it is a product state exactly when $ad = bc$ (the $2\times 2$ coefficient matrix has rank 1).

The four **Bell states** form an orthonormal basis of maximally entangled states:
$$|\Phi^\pm\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle \pm |11\rangle),\qquad |\Psi^\pm\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|01\rangle \pm |10\rangle).$$

options: Yes, it is a Bell state
Yes, because all four amplitudes are nonzero
q.name: T1
q.why: $ad = bc = \tfrac14$. Indeed it equals $|+\rangle\otimes|+\rangle$. Entanglement doesn't depend on a choice of local bases.

q.name: T2
q.prompt: The unnormalized state $|00\rangle + 2|01\rangle + 3|10\rangle + x|11\rangle$ is a product state. What is $x$?
q.why: Product requires $ad = bc$: $1\cdot x = 2\cdot 3$, so $x = 6$. It is $(|0\rangle + 3|1\rangle)\otimes(|0\rangle + 2|1\rangle)$.

steps.title: Measuring part of a system
steps.md:
Measuring qubit 1 of $\sum_{a,b} c_{ab}|ab\rangle$ in the standard basis gives outcome $a$ with probability $\sum_b |c_{ab}|^2$. The leftover state of qubit 2 is $\sum_b c_{ab}|b\rangle$, renormalized.

To measure qubit 1 in another basis $\{|e_0\rangle, |e_1\rangle\}$, first rewrite the state as $|e_0\rangle|\phi_0\rangle + |e_1\rangle|\phi_1\rangle$ (unnormalized $|\phi_k\rangle$). Then $P(k) = \langle\phi_k|\phi_k\rangle$, and qubit 2 is left in $|\phi_k\rangle/\|\phi_k\|$.

For a Bell state, measuring both qubits in the same basis (Z, X, or any real rotated basis) always gives perfectly correlated results.

q.name: T3
q.prompt: For $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(|00\rangle + |10\rangle + 2|11\rangle)$, what is the probability that the first qubit is measured as $1$?
q.why: Add $|c_{10}|^2 + |c_{11}|^2 = \tfrac16 + \tfrac46 = \tfrac56$. The second qubit is then left in $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(|0\rangle + 2|1\rangle)$.

q.name: T4
q.prompt: Alice and Bob share $|\Phi^+\rangle$. Alice measures in the $Z$ basis; Bob measures in the basis rotated by $\pi/8$, i.e. $\{\cos\tfrac{\pi}{8}|0\rangle + \sin\tfrac{\pi}{8}|1\rangle,\ -\sin\tfrac{\pi}{8}|0\rangle+\cos\tfrac{\pi}{8}|1\rangle\}$. Probability their outcomes agree?
q.why: If Alice gets 0, Bob holds $|0\rangle$ and gets his first outcome with probability $\cos^2(\pi/8)$; the case where Alice gets 1 is symmetric. This $\cos^2$ of the angle between bases is the number behind the CHSH game.

q.name: T5
q.prompt: How many complex amplitudes describe a general state of 5 qubits?
q.why: $2^5 = 32$. This exponential growth is why classical simulation of quantum systems is hard.

course.title: Classical Boolean Circuits · Reversible Boolean Circuits

unit.title: Classical and reversible circuits
unit.date: Notes: Classical Boolean Circuits · Reversible Boolean Circuits
unit.intro: Universal gate sets, the cost of irreversibility, and how Toffoli gates plus uncomputation make any classical function a clean reversible circuit.

steps.title: Boolean circuits
steps.md:
Any Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^m$ can be built from AND, OR, NOT (plus FANOUT, which copies a wire). One gate can even do it alone: **NAND** is universal, since
- $\text{NOT}(x) = \text{NAND}(x,x)$,
- $\text{AND}(x,y) = \text{NOT}(\text{NAND}(x,y))$,
- $\text{OR}(x,y) = \text{NAND}(\text{NOT }x, \text{NOT }y)$.

Counting arguments show most $n$-bit functions need about $2^n/n$ gates, so universality doesn't make every function *efficient*. Complexity theory asks which functions have polynomial-size circuits.

q.name: C1
q.prompt: Using only two-input NAND gates (inputs may be reused), what is the fewest gates needed to compute OR(x, y)?
q.why: One NAND to get $\bar x$, one to get $\bar y$, and one more: $\text{NAND}(\bar x,\bar y) = x\lor y$.

steps.title: Reversible computation
steps.md:
A gate is **reversible** if its output determines its input, so it permutes the $2^k$ bit strings. Erasing information costs energy (Landauer's principle), and quantum evolution is unitary, hence reversible. So we want reversible circuits.

- **Toffoli** (CCNOT): $(x, y, z)\mapsto(x, y, z\oplus xy)$. With $z = 0$ it computes AND; with $z = 1$ it computes NAND. Toffoli plus constant inputs is universal.
- **Fredkin** (controlled-SWAP): $(x, y, z)\mapsto(x, y, z)$ if $x=0$, and $(x, z, y)$ if $x=1$. It conserves the number of 1s.

**Garbage and uncomputation (Bennett):** compute $f$ with scratch bits, CNOT the answer onto a fresh register, then run the circuit backwards. The result is $|x\rangle|0\rangle\mapsto|x\rangle|f(x)\rangle$ with every scratch bit returned to 0.

q.name: C2
q.prompt: A Toffoli gate with target bit initialized to 1 computes which function of its controls x, y?
q.why: The target becomes $1\oplus xy = \overline{xy}$.

options: Garbage left entangled with the input destroys the interference the algorithm relies on
Garbage qubits use too much memory
Measuring garbage gives the answer away
Unitary gates cannot act on garbage qubits
q.soln: Garbage left entangled with the input destroys the interference the algorithm relies on
q.name: C3
q.prompt: Why must a quantum algorithm uncompute its scratch (garbage) qubits?
q.why: If the register holds $\sum_x |x\rangle|f(x)\rangle|g(x)\rangle$, the garbage $g(x)$ marks which branch is which. Branches with different garbage can no longer interfere, as if $x$ had been measured.

q.name: C4
q.prompt: How many different reversible gates act on 2 bits (i.e., how many permutations of the four 2-bit strings are there)?
q.why: $4! = 24$. Only some are linear over $\mathbb{F}_2$ (built from CNOTs and NOTs). No 2-bit reversible gate can build AND, which is why Toffoli needs 3 bits.

q.name: C5
q.prompt: A Fredkin gate receives (x, y, z) = (1, 0, 1). What is the output? Enter it as three bits, like 010.
q.why: The control is 1, so $y$ and $z$ swap: $(1, 1, 0)$. The number of 1s (two) is preserved.

course.title: Quantum Gates I · Quantum Gates II

unit.title: Quantum gates and universality
unit.date: Notes: Quantum Gates I · Quantum Gates II
unit.intro: CNOT and controlled gates, basis-change tricks, and why one- and two-qubit gates suffice to build any unitary.

steps.title: Two-qubit gates
steps.md:
The **CNOT** flips the target when the control is 1: $|a\rangle|b\rangle\mapsto|a\rangle|b\oplus a\rangle$. A general **controlled-$U$** applies $U$ to the target only when the control is $|1\rangle$.

Three identities you will use constantly:
- **CZ is symmetric.** $\mathrm{CZ} = \mathrm{diag}(1,1,1,-1)$; it doesn't matter which qubit you call the control.
- **Hadamards reverse a CNOT.** $(H\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CNOT}_{1\to2}\,(H\otimes H) = \mathrm{CNOT}_{2\to1}$, because in the $X$ basis the roles swap.
- **Three CNOTs make a SWAP.** $\mathrm{CNOT}_{1\to2}\mathrm{CNOT}_{2\to1}\mathrm{CNOT}_{1\to2} = \mathrm{SWAP}$.

Also $HZH = X$ and $HXH = Z$, which is why $\mathrm{CNOT} = (I\otimes H)\,\mathrm{CZ}\,(I\otimes H)$.

q.name: G1
q.prompt: What does CNOT (control = first qubit) produce from |+⟩|0⟩?
q.why: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle + |10\rangle)\mapsto\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle) = |\Phi^+\rangle$. This is the standard way to make a Bell pair.

q.name: G2
q.prompt: Apply CZ to $|+\rangle|+\rangle$, then measure both qubits in the $X$ basis. Probability of getting $(+,+)$?
q.why: $\mathrm{CZ}|{+}{+}\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle|+\rangle + |1\rangle|-\rangle)$. Its overlap with $|{+}{+}\rangle$ is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = \tfrac12$, so the probability is $\tfrac14$. In fact all four outcomes are equally likely, because the state is maximally entangled.

steps.title: Universality
steps.md:
**Exact universality:** every $n$-qubit unitary is a product of CNOTs and one-qubit gates. Every one-qubit gate decomposes as $e^{i\alpha}R_z(\beta)R_y(\gamma)R_z(\delta)$ (Euler angles).

**Approximate universality:** a finite set such as $\{H, T, \mathrm{CNOT}\}$ suffices to approximate any unitary to accuracy $\epsilon$. The **Solovay–Kitaev theorem** says only $O(\log^c(1/\epsilon))$ gates are needed per one-qubit gate, so discretizing costs only a polylogarithmic factor.

Controlled-controlled gates (Toffoli) and multiply-controlled gates are built from these using ancillas, so classical reversible circuits embed directly into quantum ones.

q.name: G3
q.prompt: Which identity is correct?
q.why: $H$ swaps the $x$ and $z$ axes of the Bloch sphere, so it conjugates $Z$ to $X$ (and $Y$ to $-Y$).

q.name: G4
q.prompt: What is the smallest $k > 0$ with $T^k = I$, where $T = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{i\pi/4})$?
q.why: $T^k = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{ik\pi/4})$ equals $I$ first at $k = 8$. Along the way $T^2 = S$ and $T^4 = Z$.

q.name: G5
q.prompt: Three CNOTs alternating control and target (1→2, 2→1, 1→2) implement which gate?
q.why: On basis states this is the XOR-swap trick: $(a,b)\to(a, a\oplus b)\to(b, a\oplus b)\to(b, a)$.

unit.title: Teleportation, superdense coding and no-cloning
unit.intro: Entanglement as a resource: sending a qubit with two classical bits, sending two bits with one qubit, and why unknown states can't be copied.

steps.title: No-cloning
steps.md:
No unitary can map $|\psi\rangle|0\rangle\mapsto|\psi\rangle|\psi\rangle$ for every $|\psi\rangle$. Unitaries preserve inner products, so this would require $\langle\phi|\psi\rangle = \langle\phi|\psi\rangle^2$, which forces the overlap to be 0 or 1. You *can* copy states from a known orthogonal set (CNOT copies $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$), but not arbitrary or non-orthogonal ones.

Imperfect cloners exist, and computing how well they do is a classic exercise in measurement probabilities.

steps.title: Teleportation
steps.md:
Alice holds $|\psi\rangle$, and she shares $|\Phi^+\rangle$ with Bob.

1. Alice measures her two qubits ($|\psi\rangle$ and her half of the pair) in the **Bell basis**. Each of the 4 outcomes has probability $\tfrac14$, *whatever* $|\psi\rangle$ is.
2. She sends the 2-bit result to Bob.
3. Bob's qubit is now $X^bZ^a|\psi\rangle$ for the reported bits $a, b$, so he undoes that.

Nothing travels faster than light: until the bits arrive, Bob's qubit is maximally mixed. An eavesdropper on the classical channel sees uniformly random bits and learns nothing. Alice's copy is destroyed, consistent with no-cloning.

q.name: P1
q.prompt: In teleportation, what is the probability of any particular one of Alice's four Bell-measurement outcomes?
q.why: Rewriting $|\psi\rangle|\Phi^+\rangle$ in the Bell basis on Alice's side gives four terms, each with amplitude $\tfrac12$, independent of $|\psi\rangle$. That independence is why the classical bits carry no information about $|\psi\rangle$.

steps.title: Superdense coding
steps.md:
Teleportation run in reverse: if Alice and Bob share $|\Phi^+\rangle$, Alice can send **two classical bits** by transmitting **one qubit**. She applies $I$, $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$ to her half, which turns the pair into one of the four Bell states, and sends it. Bob does a Bell measurement.

The resource tally:

| protocol | uses | delivers |
|---|---|---|
| teleportation | 1 ebit + 2 bits | 1 qubit |
| superdense coding | 1 ebit + 1 qubit | 2 bits |

Without shared entanglement, one qubit can carry at most one bit (Holevo's bound).

options: Nothing: his qubit's density matrix is I/2 for every |ψ⟩
Everything, up to a Pauli error
q.soln: Nothing: his qubit's density matrix is I/2 for every |ψ⟩
q.name: P2
q.prompt: Before Alice's classical bits arrive, what can Bob learn about |ψ⟩ from his qubit?
q.why: Averaging $X^bZ^a|\psi\rangle$ over the four equally likely outcomes gives $I/2$. This no-signaling property is why teleportation can't send information faster than light.

q.name: P3
q.prompt: Alice and Bob share |Φ+⟩. Alice applies Z to her qubit and sends it to Bob, who does a Bell measurement. What does he find?
q.why: $(Z\otimes I)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle + |11\rangle) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|00\rangle - |11\rangle)$. This is superdense coding's encoding for one of the four 2-bit messages.

q.name: P4
q.prompt: How many classical bits does superdense coding deliver per qubit sent (with one shared Bell pair)?
q.why: Alice's four local operations map $|\Phi^+\rangle$ to the four orthogonal Bell states, which Bob distinguishes perfectly: $\log_2 4 = 2$ bits.

course.title: Density Matrices I · Density Matrices II

unit.title: Density matrices and partial trace
unit.date: Notes: Density Matrices I · Density Matrices II
unit.intro: Mixed states, the Bloch ball, and how to describe one half of an entangled pair.

steps.title: Ensembles and density matrices
steps.md:
If a system is in $|\psi_i\rangle$ with probability $p_i$, its **density matrix** is
$$\rho = \sum_i p_i\,|\psi_i\rangle\langle\psi_i|.$$
Every measurement statistic depends only on $\rho$: $P(k) = \mathrm{Tr}(\Pi_k\rho)$ and $\langle M\rangle = \mathrm{Tr}(M\rho)$. **Different ensembles with the same $\rho$ are physically indistinguishable.** For example, $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ and $\{|+\rangle, |-\rangle\}$, each with probabilities $\tfrac12$, both give $I/2$.

A valid $\rho$ is Hermitian, positive semidefinite, and has trace 1. It is **pure** iff $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho^2 = 1$; otherwise $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho^2 < 1$.

steps.title: The Bloch ball
steps.md:
Every qubit density matrix can be written
$$\rho = \tfrac12\left(I + r_xX + r_yY + r_zZ\right),\qquad |\vec r| \le 1,$$
with $r_x = \langle X\rangle$, and so on. Pure states lie on the surface and mixed states inside; $I/2$ is the center. Purity is $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho^2 = \tfrac12(1 + |\vec r|^2)$.

The Bloch vector of a mixture is the probability-weighted average of the Bloch vectors, which makes "same density matrix?" questions quick.

q.name: D1
q.prompt: What is $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho^2$ for the ensemble $\{|0\rangle$ w.p. $\tfrac12$, $|+\rangle$ w.p. $\tfrac12\}$?
q.why: The average Bloch vector is $\tfrac12(0,0,1) + \tfrac12(1,0,0) = (\tfrac12, 0, \tfrac12)$, with $|\vec r|^2 = \tfrac12$. So $\mathrm{Tr}\,\rho^2 = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac12) = \tfrac34$.

steps.title: Partial trace
steps.md:
For a joint state $\rho_{AB}$, Alice's local description is the **reduced density matrix** $\rho_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B\,\rho_{AB}$. In components,
$$(\rho_A)_{aa'} = \sum_b (\rho_{AB})_{ab,\,a'b}.$$
For a pure state $\sum c_{ab}|ab\rangle$, this is $\rho_A = CC^\dagger$, where $C$ is the coefficient matrix.

- For any Bell state, $\rho_A = I/2$: maximal entanglement means maximal local ignorance.
- **No-signaling:** nothing Bob does locally (unitaries, or measurements whose results he keeps to himself) changes $\rho_A$.
- If Bob measures and tells Alice the result, her conditional states form an ensemble whose average is $\rho_A$.

q.name: D2
q.prompt: For $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(|00\rangle + |01\rangle + |10\rangle)$, what is the off-diagonal entry $\langle 0|\rho_A|1\rangle$ of $\rho_A = \mathrm{Tr}_B\,\rho$?
q.why: $C = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $\rho_A = CC^\dagger = \tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. The off-diagonal entry is $\tfrac13$.

q.name: D3
q.prompt: For $\rho = \tfrac34|0\rangle\langle0| + \tfrac14|1\rangle\langle1|$, what is $\mathrm{Tr}(Z\rho)$?
q.why: $\tfrac34(1) + \tfrac14(-1) = \tfrac12$.

q.name: D4
q.prompt: Which ensemble has density matrix I/2?
q.why: Antipodal Bloch vectors $\pm\hat y$ with equal weights average to $\vec 0$, the center of the ball, which is $I/2$.

course.title: The GHZ Experiment (Theory) · Quantum Optics and the GHZ Experiment

unit.title: Nonlocality: CHSH and GHZ
unit.date: Notes: The GHZ Experiment (Theory) · Quantum Optics and the GHZ Experiment
unit.intro: Why entanglement can't be explained by pre-agreed classical answers, first statistically (CHSH) and then in a single shot (GHZ).

steps.title: Local hidden variables and CHSH
steps.md:
A **local hidden-variable** (LHV) model says each particle carries pre-set answers to every measurement it might face, and no influence passes between distant labs.

In the **CHSH game**, a referee sends random bits $x, y$ to Alice and Bob, who answer $a, b$ without communicating. They win if $a\oplus b = x\wedge y$.

- With any classical (LHV) strategy, the best win rate is $3/4$.
- Sharing $|\Phi^+\rangle$ and measuring in bases at angles $0, \pi/4$ (Alice) and $\pi/8, -\pi/8$ (Bob) wins with probability $\cos^2(\pi/8)\approx 0.854$.

Equivalently, the CHSH correlation $S$ satisfies $|S| \le 2$ classically and reaches $2\sqrt2$ quantumly (Tsirelson's bound).

q.name: H1
q.prompt: What is the optimal quantum win probability of the CHSH game?
q.why: Each pair of bases is $\pi/8$ apart (or $3\pi/8$ in the case that needs anti-correlation), so every case is won with probability $\cos^2(\pi/8)$.

steps.title: The GHZ argument
steps.md:
Take the three-qubit **GHZ state** $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|000\rangle + |111\rangle)$. It is an eigenstate of
$$XXX \text{ with eigenvalue } +1,\qquad XYY,\ YXY,\ YYX \text{ each with eigenvalue } -1.$$
Suppose each qubit carried pre-set values $x_j, y_j\in\{\pm1\}$. Multiplying the three $-1$ equations gives $x_Ax_Bx_C(y_Ay_By_C)^2 = -1$, so $x_Ax_Bx_C = -1$. But quantum mechanics predicts $+1$, *every time*.

So GHZ refutes local hidden variables with certainty in principle, rather than statistically like CHSH. Experiments use polarization-entangled photons from parametric down-conversion; imperfect detectors open loopholes that careful experiments must close.

q.name: H2
q.prompt: In the GHZ state, what is the (certain) product of the three outcomes when Alice, Bob and Charlie measure $X$, $Y$, $Y$ respectively?
q.why: $Y|0\rangle = i|1\rangle$ and $Y|1\rangle = -i|0\rangle$, so $XYY|000\rangle = (i)(i)|111\rangle = -|111\rangle$ and $XYY|111\rangle = -|000\rangle$. The eigenvalue is $-1$.

q.name: H3
q.prompt: What is the best a classical (local hidden-variable) strategy can do in the CHSH game?
q.why: Always answering $a = b = 0$ wins 3 of the 4 input pairs, and checking all 16 deterministic strategies shows none does better. Shared randomness only mixes deterministic strategies, so it doesn't help.

options: It gives a contradiction with certainty, not just a statistical violation
q.soln: It gives a contradiction with certainty, not just a statistical violation
q.name: H4
q.prompt: How does the GHZ argument differ from CHSH?
q.why: With GHZ, every run of the $XXX$ measurement contradicts the LHV prediction. With CHSH, LHV models win the game 75% of the time and quantum mechanics only raises that rate.

course.title: The Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm · Classical Computational Complexity Theory

unit.title: Deutsch–Jozsa and complexity classes
unit.date: Notes: The Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm · Classical Computational Complexity Theory
unit.intro: Phase kickback, the first exponential oracle separation, and where BQP sits among classical complexity classes.

steps.title: Oracles and phase kickback
steps.md:
A classical function $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ is given as the reversible **oracle** $U_f|x\rangle|y\rangle = |x\rangle|y\oplus f(x)\rangle$.

If the target is $|-\rangle$, then $U_f|x\rangle|-\rangle = (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle|-\rangle$: the function value is **kicked back** as a phase. One query to a uniform superposition then produces
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x (-1)^{f(x)}|x\rangle.$$

steps.title: Deutsch–Jozsa
steps.md:
**Promise:** $f$ is constant or balanced (0 on exactly half the inputs). **Circuit:** $H^{\otimes n}$, phase oracle, $H^{\otimes n}$, measure. Using $H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle = 2^{-n/2}\sum_y(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle$, the amplitude of $|y\rangle$ is
$$\frac{1}{2^n}\sum_x (-1)^{f(x) + x\cdot y}.$$
For $y = 0^n$ this is the average of $(-1)^{f(x)}$: $\pm1$ if $f$ is constant and $0$ if balanced. So one query decides with certainty. A deterministic classical algorithm needs $2^{n-1}+1$ queries in the worst case, though a randomized one with small error needs only a few, so the speedup is mainly over exact classical computation.

The same circuit solves **Bernstein–Vazirani**: if $f(x) = s\cdot x \bmod 2$, the output is exactly $s$.

q.name: J1
q.prompt: Run Deutsch–Jozsa with $n = 3$ on a function that equals 1 on exactly 2 of the 8 inputs (so the promise fails). What is the probability of measuring $000$?
q.why: The amplitude of $|000\rangle$ is $\tfrac18(6\cdot(+1) + 2\cdot(-1)) = \tfrac12$, so the probability is $\tfrac14$.

q.name: J2
q.prompt: In Bernstein–Vazirani with hidden string s = 101, what string does the circuit output? (Enter the bits, like 011.)
q.why: The phase state is $\sum_x(-1)^{s\cdot x}|x\rangle = H^{\otimes n}|s\rangle$, so the final Hadamards return exactly $|s\rangle$.

steps.title: Complexity classes
steps.md:
- **P**: solvable in polynomial time. **BPP**: polynomial time with randomness and bounded error.
- **NP**: "yes" answers have short certificates you can check efficiently.
- **BQP**: solvable by polynomial-size quantum circuits with bounded error.

Known: $\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}$. Factoring is in BQP but not believed to be in BPP. Nobody believes $\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}$: Grover's algorithm gives only a quadratic speedup for brute-force search, and that is optimal.

Oracle results (Deutsch–Jozsa, Simon) prove separations *relative to an oracle*, not unconditional separations.

q.name: J3
q.prompt: Which containment is known to hold?
q.why: A quantum circuit's acceptance probability can be computed by summing over paths in polynomial space. The other three are open, and believed false.

q.name: J4
q.prompt: For $n = 4$, how many queries does a deterministic classical algorithm need in the worst case to decide constant vs. balanced with certainty?
q.why: After $2^{n-1} = 8$ equal answers the function could still be balanced, so you need $2^{n-1}+1 = 9$.

unit.title: Simon's algorithm
unit.intro: An exponential speedup for finding a hidden XOR period, the blueprint for Shor's algorithm.

steps.title: The problem and the circuit
steps.md:
**Promise:** $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n$ satisfies $f(x) = f(y) \iff y \in\{x, x\oplus s\}$ for a hidden $s\ne 0$. **Goal:** find $s$.

**One round:**
1. Prepare $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_x|x\rangle|0\rangle$ and query: $\sum_x|x\rangle|f(x)\rangle$.
2. Measure the second register. The first collapses to $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|x_0\rangle + |x_0\oplus s\rangle)$ for a random $x_0$.
3. Apply $H^{\otimes n}$ and measure. You get a uniformly random $y$ with $y\cdot s = 0 \pmod 2$.

Each round gives one linear equation for $s$. After about $n$ rounds you have $n-1$ independent equations, and Gaussian elimination over $\mathbb{F}_2$ gives $s$.

q.name: S1
q.prompt: For $n = 4$ and $s \neq 0$, how many different strings $y$ can a round of Simon's algorithm output?
q.why: $y$ ranges over the strings orthogonal to $s$, which form a subspace of dimension $n - 1$, so there are $2^{n-1} = 8$, all equally likely.

q.name: S2
q.prompt: With n = 3, two rounds return y₁ = 110 and y₂ = 011. What is s ≠ 000? (Enter the bits.)
q.why: $s\cdot110 = 0$ gives $s_1 = s_2$, and $s\cdot011 = 0$ gives $s_2 = s_3$, so the only nonzero solution is $s = 111$.

steps.title: Why it's fast
steps.md:
Classically, you learn about $s$ only by finding a **collision** $f(x) = f(x')$, and then $s = x\oplus x'$. By the birthday paradox that takes about $2^{n/2}$ queries, and this is provably necessary even with randomness. Simon needs $O(n)$ queries plus polynomial classical post-processing, an **exponential** oracle separation between BQP and BPP.

Shor's algorithm follows the same pattern with $\mathbb{Z}_N$ in place of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$: superpose, query a periodic function, Fourier transform, sample the dual of the period, and solve classically.

q.name: S3
q.prompt: How does the number of classical queries needed for Simon's problem grow?
q.why: Collisions appear after about $\sqrt{2^n}$ random queries, and no classical strategy does much better.

q.name: S4
q.prompt: For $n = 5$, what is the probability that a round outputs one particular valid $y$?
q.why: There are $2^{n-1} = 16$ valid strings, each equally likely.

options: The uniform superposition over all x
q.name: S5
q.prompt: After measuring the second register (value f(x₀)), what is the state of the first register?
q.why: Exactly two inputs map to $f(x_0)$: $x_0$ and $x_0\oplus s$. The measurement leaves their equal superposition.

course.title: The Quantum Fourier Transform · Phase Estimation

unit.title: QFT and phase estimation
unit.date: Notes: The Quantum Fourier Transform · Phase Estimation
unit.intro: The Fourier transform on $2^n$ amplitudes with $O(n^2)$ gates, and its main use: reading off an eigenvalue's phase.

steps.title: The quantum Fourier transform
steps.md:
With $N = 2^n$ and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/N}$,
$$\mathrm{QFT}_N|j\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\omega^{jk}|k\rangle.$$
It factors into a product of single-qubit states, $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt N}\bigotimes_{\ell}\left(|0\rangle + e^{2\pi i\, j/2^\ell}|1\rangle\right)$. That gives a circuit of Hadamards and controlled phase rotations $R_k = \mathrm{diag}(1, e^{2\pi i/2^k})$ with $O(n^2)$ gates, plus a final bit reversal.

Caveat: this does *not* compute a classical FFT exponentially faster. The output amplitudes can't be read out; you can only sample from them.

q.name: F1
q.prompt: Apply $\mathrm{QFT}_4$ to $|1\rangle$. What is the amplitude of $|2\rangle$?
q.why: $\omega = i$ for $N = 4$, so the amplitudes are $\tfrac12(1, i, -1, -i)$. The coefficient of $|2\rangle$ is $\tfrac12 i^2 = -\tfrac12$.

steps.title: Phase estimation
steps.md:
Given a unitary $U$ with eigenvector $|u\rangle$, $U|u\rangle = e^{2\pi i\varphi}|u\rangle$, estimate $\varphi\in[0,1)$:

1. Put $t$ ancilla qubits in uniform superposition.
2. Apply controlled-$U^{2^k}$ from ancilla $k$. Kickback leaves $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2^t}}\sum_j e^{2\pi i\varphi j}|j\rangle$.
3. Apply $\mathrm{QFT}^{-1}$ and measure an integer $m$; the estimate is $\varphi\approx m/2^t$.

If $\varphi = m/2^t$ exactly, the output is $m$ with certainty. Otherwise the nearest $t$-bit approximation appears with probability at least $4/\pi^2\approx 0.405$, and adding a few ancilla qubits boosts confidence.

q.name: F2
q.prompt: Phase estimation with $t = 3$ ancillas and $\varphi = 0.375$. What integer $m$ is measured?
q.why: $0.375 = 3/8 = 0.011_2$ is exactly representable with 3 bits, so $m = 3$ with certainty.

q.name: F3
q.prompt: With $t = 4$ ancillas, how many applications of $U$ in total do the controlled-$U^{2^k}$ steps use (counting $U^{2^k}$ as $2^k$ uses)?
q.why: $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 2^t - 1 = 15$. When $U^{2^k}$ can be computed directly (as in modular exponentiation), the cost is far smaller.

q.name: F4
q.prompt: What is QFT_N|0⟩?
q.why: With $j = 0$, every phase $\omega^{0} = 1$.

q.name: F5
q.prompt: If $\varphi$ is not a multiple of $1/2^t$, what lower bound holds on the probability of getting the closest $t$-bit estimate?
q.why: The output distribution is a discrete sinc-squared peak, and the worst case ($\varphi$ exactly between two grid points) gives $4/\pi^2$.

course.title: Quantum Factoring Algorithm · Number Theory for the Factoring Algorithm · The Discrete Log Algorithm

unit.title: Factoring and discrete log
unit.date: Notes: Quantum Factoring Algorithm · Number Theory for the Factoring Algorithm · The Discrete Log Algorithm
unit.intro: Reduce factoring to order finding, solve order finding with phase estimation, and recover the order with continued fractions.

steps.title: Factoring reduces to order finding
steps.md:
To factor an odd $N$ that isn't a prime power:

1. Pick a random $a$ with $1 < a < N$. If $\gcd(a, N) > 1$, you've already found a factor.
2. Find the **order** $r$: the least $r > 0$ with $a^r\equiv 1 \pmod N$ (the quantum step).
3. If $r$ is even and $a^{r/2}\not\equiv -1 \pmod N$, then $\gcd(a^{r/2}\pm1, N)$ are nontrivial factors.

This works because $(a^{r/2}-1)(a^{r/2}+1)\equiv 0$ but neither factor is $\equiv 0$, so $N$ shares a factor with each. For a random $a$, step 3 succeeds with probability at least $1/2$.

q.name: R1
q.prompt: What is the order of $a = 7$ modulo $N = 15$?

q.name: R2
q.prompt: What is the order of $a = 2$ modulo $N = 21$?

steps.title: Order finding as phase estimation
steps.md:
Let $U_a|x\rangle = |ax \bmod N\rangle$. Its eigenvectors $|u_s\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_k e^{-2\pi i sk/r}|a^k\rangle$ have eigenvalues $e^{2\pi i s/r}$, and $|1\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt r}\sum_s|u_s\rangle$. So phase estimation started on $|1\rangle$ returns $m\approx 2^t\, s/r$ for a uniformly random $s$.

**Recovering $r$:** use $t\approx 2\log_2 N$ bits, so that $s/r$ is the unique fraction with denominator below $N$ near $m/2^t$. Find it with **continued fractions**. If $\gcd(s, r) > 1$ you get a factor of $r$; repeating a few times fixes that.

The cost is dominated by modular exponentiation, $O(n^3)$ gates with schoolbook arithmetic, so factoring runs in polynomial time.

q.name: R3
q.prompt: With $t = 8$, phase estimation for $U_a$ returns $m = 192$. Continued fractions on $192/256$ suggest which order $r$?
q.why: $192/256 = 3/4$ exactly, so $s/r = 3/4$, giving $r = 4$ (or a multiple of 4 if $\gcd(s, r) > 1$).

steps.title: Discrete logarithm
steps.md:
Given a generator $g$ of $\mathbb{Z}_p^*$ and $b = g^a \bmod p$, find $a$. Shor's method uses two registers over $\mathbb{Z}_{p-1}$: compute $|x\rangle|y\rangle|g^xb^{-y}\rangle$, Fourier transform both registers, and measure a pair $(c, d)$ with $d\equiv ac \pmod{p-1}$ (up to the usual details). When $c$ is invertible, $a = d\,c^{-1}$.

This is an abelian **hidden subgroup problem**, like Simon and order finding, and the same idea breaks Diffie–Hellman and elliptic-curve cryptography.

q.name: R4
q.prompt: What is the order of $a = 4$ modulo $15$?

options: If gcd(a, N) > 1 you already have a factor, and a has no order mod N
To make sure r is even
To choose the number of ancilla qubits
Because U_a is not unitary otherwise
q.soln: If gcd(a, N) > 1 you already have a factor, and a has no order mod N
q.name: R5
q.prompt: In Shor's algorithm, why check gcd(a, N) before running the quantum step?
q.why: $a^r\equiv1 \pmod N$ is only possible when $a$ is invertible mod $N$, that is, when $\gcd(a, N) = 1$.

course.title: Grover's Search Algorithm · Proof that Grover Search is Optimal · Hamiltonian Simulation

unit.title: Grover search and Hamiltonian simulation
unit.date: Notes: Grover's Search Algorithm · Proof that Grover Search is Optimal · Hamiltonian Simulation
unit.intro: Search $N$ items in $O(\sqrt N)$ queries, why you can't beat that, and how to simulate $e^{-iHt}$ with gates.

steps.title: Grover's algorithm as a rotation
steps.md:
Start in the uniform superposition $|s\rangle$ over $N$ items, of which $M$ are marked. One **Grover iteration** is the phase oracle (flip the sign of marked items) followed by the diffusion $2|s\rangle\langle s| - I$.

Everything happens in the plane spanned by $|\text{good}\rangle$ and $|\text{bad}\rangle$. With $\sin\theta = \sqrt{M/N}$, each iteration rotates by $2\theta$, so after $k$ iterations
$$P(\text{success}) = \sin^2\big((2k+1)\theta\big).$$
The best choice is $k\approx\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt{N/M}$. Iterating more *overshoots* and the success probability falls again.

q.name: W1
q.prompt: Grover with $N = 4$ items and $M = 1$ marked. What is the success probability after one iteration?
q.why: $\sin\theta = 1/2$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$ and $3\theta = 90^\circ$. One iteration finds the item with certainty.

q.name: W2
q.prompt: Grover with $N = 8$, $M = 1$. Success probability after one iteration?
q.why: $\sin\theta = 1/\sqrt8$, and $\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta = \tfrac{3}{\sqrt8} - \tfrac{4}{8\sqrt8} = \tfrac{5}{2\sqrt8}$. Squared, that is $\tfrac{25}{32}$.

steps.title: Grover is optimal
steps.md:
The **BBBV hybrid argument:** run any $T$-query algorithm on the empty oracle and on an oracle that marks item $x$. Each query can move the state by an amount proportional to the amplitude on $x$. Summed over all $N$ choices of $x$, the total "query magnitude" is at most $T$, so for some $x$ the two runs differ by $O(T/\sqrt N)$. Telling the two oracles apart reliably therefore needs $T = \Omega(\sqrt N)$.

Consequence: brute-force search gives only a quadratic speedup. Black-box quantum algorithms can't solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time.

steps.title: Hamiltonian simulation
steps.md:
Physics gives $U(t) = e^{-iHt}$ for a Hermitian $H$. For a local Hamiltonian $H = \sum_j H_j$, where each term acts on a few qubits, use the **Trotter–Suzuki** product
$$e^{-iHt}\approx\Big(\prod_j e^{-iH_jt/n}\Big)^n,$$
with error $O(t^2/n)$ from the commutators. (There is no error at all if the terms commute.) To reach error $\epsilon$, take $n = O(t^2/\epsilon)$ steps; higher-order formulas do better.

Building blocks: $e^{-i\alpha Z\otimes Z}$ is CNOT, then $R_z(2\alpha)$ on the target, then CNOT. Conjugating by $H$ gates turns $Z$s into $X$s. This was Feynman's original motivation for quantum computers.

q.name: W3
q.prompt: For $N = 2^{20}$ and one marked item, about how many Grover iterations are optimal? (Use $\frac{\pi}{4}\sqrt N$.)
q.why: $\sqrt{2^{20}} = 1024$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot1024\approx804$, compared with about half a million classical queries on average.

options: The success probability drops back near 0
The algorithm outputs two marked items
q.soln: The success probability drops back near 0
q.name: W4
q.prompt: What happens if you run about twice the optimal number of Grover iterations?
q.why: After $2k$ iterations the state has rotated by about $\pi$ instead of $\pi/2$, so it sits back near $|\text{bad}\rangle$.

options: When all the terms H_j commute
When each H_j is a Pauli operator
q.soln: When all the terms H_j commute
q.name: W5
q.prompt: When is the first-order Trotter formula exact?
q.why: If the terms commute, $e^{-i(A+B)t} = e^{-iAt}e^{-iBt}$ exactly, so the commutator error terms vanish.

course.title: Intro to QECC: the 9-Qubit Code · More on the 9-Qubit Code · The 7-Qubit Hamming Code · Quantum CSS Codes

unit.title: Quantum error correction
unit.date: Notes: Intro to QECC: the 9-Qubit Code · More on the 9-Qubit Code · The 7-Qubit Hamming Code · Quantum CSS Codes
unit.intro: Discretizing errors, Shor's 9-qubit code, the Steane code, and the CSS construction.

steps.title: Correcting quantum errors at all
steps.md:
Three obstacles look fatal: no-cloning (can't copy), continuous errors, and measurement disturbing the state. The fixes:

- **Redundancy without copying:** encode $\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\mapsto\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle$. That is entanglement, not three copies.
- **Measure only the syndrome:** $Z_1Z_2$ and $Z_2Z_3$ reveal *which* qubit flipped, never $\alpha$ or $\beta$.
- **Errors discretize:** any single-qubit error is a combination of $I, X, Y, Z$. Measuring the syndrome collapses the error onto one of these, so correcting $X$ and $Z$ errors corrects *every* single-qubit error.

The bit-flip code corrects one $X$. The same code in the Hadamard basis ($|{+}{+}{+}\rangle$, $|{-}{-}{-}\rangle$) corrects one $Z$.

q.name: E1
q.prompt: In the 3-qubit bit-flip code the syndrome is $Z_1Z_2 = -1$, $Z_2Z_3 = +1$. Which qubit flipped? (Enter 1, 2, or 3.)
q.why: Qubits 1 and 2 disagree while 2 and 3 agree, so qubit 1 is the odd one out.

steps.title: Shor's 9-qubit code
steps.md:
Concatenate the two 3-qubit codes:
$$|0_L\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}(|000\rangle+|111\rangle)^{\otimes3},\qquad |1_L\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}(|000\rangle-|111\rangle)^{\otimes3}.$$
Within each block, $ZZ$ checks catch bit flips. Comparing the signs of the three blocks (with $X^{\otimes6}$-type checks) catches phase flips. So it corrects any single-qubit error.

It is **degenerate**: $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ act identically on the code space, so the decoder needn't know which of them happened.

steps.title: Steane and CSS codes
steps.md:
The classical **Hamming [7,4,3] code** has a parity-check matrix whose columns are the binary numbers 1–7. The syndrome of a single bit flip *is the binary position* of the flipped bit.

A **CSS code** uses classical codes $C_2\subset C_1$. Bit flips are corrected with $C_1$ and phase flips with $C_2^\perp$, which works because a Hadamard swaps the roles of $X$ and $Z$. With $C_1 = $ Hamming and $C_2 = C_1^\perp$, you get the **Steane $[[7,1,3]]$ code**: 7 physical qubits, 1 logical qubit, distance 3 (corrects any single error), and 6 stabilizer generators (3 $X$-type, 3 $Z$-type).

q.name: E2
q.prompt: In the Hamming [7,4,3] code with columns 1–7 in binary, a single bit flip gives syndrome 101. Which bit position flipped?
q.why: The syndrome equals the column of the flipped bit, and $101_2 = 5$.

q.name: E3
q.prompt: How many physical qubits does the Steane code use to encode one logical qubit?
q.why: It's $[[7,1,3]]$, smaller than Shor's 9 qubits. The smallest code that corrects any single-qubit error uses 5.

options: Different errors (e.g. Z₁ and Z₂) act the same on the code space
q.soln: Different errors (e.g. Z₁ and Z₂) act the same on the code space
q.name: E4
q.prompt: Why is Shor's 9-qubit code called degenerate?
q.why: $Z_1Z_2$ is a stabilizer, so $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ have the same effect on code states and can share a correction.

q.name: E5
q.prompt: How many independent stabilizer generators does an [[n, k]] stabilizer code have when n = 7, k = 1?
q.why: $n - k = 6$. Each generator halves the space: $2^7/2^6 = 2$ dimensions, one logical qubit.

course.title: The BB84 Quantum Key Distribution Protocol and the Proof of Its Security

unit.title: BB84 quantum key distribution
unit.date: Notes: The BB84 Quantum Key Distribution Protocol and the Proof of Its Security
unit.intro: Share a secret key whose security rests on quantum mechanics, and see why eavesdropping can't go unnoticed.

steps.title: The protocol
steps.md:
1. Alice sends random bits, each in a random basis: $Z$ ($|0\rangle, |1\rangle$) or $X$ ($|+\rangle, |-\rangle$).
2. Bob measures each qubit in a random basis.
3. Over a public but **authenticated** classical channel, they compare bases (not bits) and keep the positions where the bases matched. This **sifting** keeps about half.
4. They reveal a random sample of the sifted bits to estimate the error rate. If it's too high, they abort.
5. **Error correction** fixes the remaining mismatches. **Privacy amplification** (hashing) shrinks the key so Eve's partial information becomes negligible.

q.name: K1
q.prompt: On average, what fraction of the transmitted qubits survive sifting?
q.why: Bob's random basis matches Alice's with probability $\tfrac12$.

steps.title: Why eavesdropping shows
steps.md:
In an **intercept–resend** attack, Eve measures in a random basis and resends what she saw. On a sifted bit, she picks the wrong basis half the time. Then Bob's result is random, wrong half of those times. So Eve introduces a $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14$ error rate while learning only about half the bits.

More generally, information gain forces disturbance (no-cloning again). The **Shor–Preskill proof** relates BB84 to a CSS code. Error correction and privacy amplification are the classical shadow of decoding a CSS code, which gives a secure key rate of $1 - 2h(e)$, where $h$ is binary entropy. That stays positive up to an error rate of about 11%.

q.name: K2
q.prompt: What error rate does a full intercept–resend attack (random bases) cause on the sifted key?
q.why: Wrong basis with probability $\tfrac12$, then a random result: $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14$.

q.name: K3
q.prompt: If Eve does intercept–resend on only 40% of the qubits, what is the expected error rate on the sifted key?
q.why: $0.4\times\tfrac14 = 0.1$.

options: Otherwise Eve can impersonate Bob to Alice and vice versa (man-in-the-middle)
To keep the basis choices secret
Because the qubits carry no information
q.soln: Otherwise Eve can impersonate Bob to Alice and vice versa (man-in-the-middle)
q.name: K4
q.prompt: Why must the classical channel be authenticated?
q.why: QKD protects against eavesdropping on the quantum channel, but without authentication Eve could run separate QKD sessions with each party. So QKD needs a short shared secret to start; it expands a key rather than creating one from nothing.
